segments.text: [style: brisk, clear, architectural voice; steady studio cadence] Book Two, Proposition Two. If a segment be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and both of the segments is equal to the square on the whole. Let the segment A B be cut at random at the point C.

segments.style: speaking briskly, nimble, crisp, and composed
segments.text: [style: methodical, precise constructive cadence] On A B, describe the square A D E B by One Forty-Six. Through C, draw C F parallel to A D or B E by One Thirty-One.

segments.style: speaking briskly, nimble, crisp, and composed
segments.text: [style: luminous, deductive geometric clarity] Then the whole square A E equals the sum of the rectangles A F and C E, and A E is the square on A B. Because A D equals A B, A F is the rectangle contained by A B and A C; and because B E equals A B, C E is the rectangle contained by A B and B C. Therefore, the rectangle contained by A B and A C together with the rectangle contained by A B and B C equals the square on A B. Which was to be proved.

segments.text: [style: reflective, scholarly, architectural synthesis] If a whole segment a is partitioned into b and c, Proposition Two Two proves that a squared equals a b plus a c. As Heath observes, Euclid already used this visual partitioning in the proof of the Pythagorean theorem, One Forty-Seven, and proves the first ten propositions of Book Two independently from first principles to reveal every identity directly to the eye. In the GEOMETOR G-Index, node G eighty-three synthesizes five direct prerequisites—including square construction from One Forty-Six and parallel lines from One Thirty-One—across fifty-four ancestor nodes.
